newsitem.title: DUBAI: Perry heads to Gulf to shore up coalition.
newsitem.headline: Perry heads to Gulf to shore up coalition.

text.p: U.S. Defence Secretary William Perry headed to the Gulf on Saturday to try to secure Arab support for a possible military showdown with Iraq and rebuild the U.S.-led coalition against President Saddam Hussein.
Two U.S. missile attacks on Iraq last week failed to win broad-based international support and fragmented the coalition.

Iraq declared on Friday it would "suspend" its missile attacks on U.S. and allied aircraft policing no-fly zones over Iraq but President Bill Clinton nevertheless ordered 5,000 more troops to Kuwait and sent Perry on his regional tour.
Stops in Kuwait, focus of a rapid buildup of American armed forces, and Saudi Arabia, Washington's chief strategic ally in the Middle East, were scheduled for Perry's tour.
Kuwait, invaded by Iraq in 1990, is providing facilities for the U.S. buildup. Eight radar-dodging Stealth bombers landed in the small oil state late on Friday.
But Saudi Arabia, launchpad for the U.S.-led coalition that expelled Iraq from Kuwait in 1991, has refused to join in the new assembly of arms and men ranged against Iraq.
"I imagine the Saudis will welcome some consultation," a Western diplomat in the Saudi capital Riyadh said.
"The Saudis are concerned about the effects of the U.S. action on the coalition and anything that helps keep the coalition together will be welcome to the Saudis," he said.
"They have reservations about the U.S. action but are more concerned about the coalition sticking together. They're not too happy about the French and Russian positions either."

U.S. officials said Perry was also likely to visit Bahrain, administrative headquarters of the U.S. Fifth Fleet, and Turkey, where U.S. warplanes fly from NATO bases to enforce a no-fly zone over northern Iraq.
Saudi Arabia and Turkey have refused to let the United States use U.S. attack planes based in their countries in any raid against Iraq.
Perry's mission, as U.S. fighters, bombers, warships and troops mustered in the Gulf region, was intended to build backing for possible further U.S. attacks.

"The purpose of the Perry trip would be to talk to regional players...(about) providing the support we would need to carry out various operations in the region and to explain exactly what possible missions might be, in this case to keep the no-fly zone effectively in force," a U.S. official in Washington said.
France, whose air force takes part in Operation Southern Watch patrols over southern Iraq, criticised last week's U.S. missile strikes.
Russia opposes U.S. threats of renewed attacks. It said further action would require U.N. Security Council approval.
"He (Perry) will be coming out to put the U.S. strategy in context: the need to contain Saddam Hussein. Maybe that's not been well articulated," the Western diplomat said.

"People forget that it was as recently as 1994 when Saddam made another move on Kuwait and had to be deterred by a firm coalition response. That's the context: just remind people that Saddam is a dangerous animal. We want to remind them that we remain committed to Iraq's territorial sovereignty and integrity. There's a job to be done in restating the case. Maybe memories are shorter than you would have thought."
U.S. aircraft on Saturday continued patrols to enforce the no-fly zone over southern Iraq, encountering no threats, U.S. spokesman Lieutenant Colonel Andrew Bourland said.

"Things were very quiet in the last 24 hours over the no-fly zone," he told Reuters by telephone from Riyadh. "In fact it was almost inconsequential activity that we detected from the Iraqis. We detected some minor surface-to-air radar capability. It was just very minor electronic activity we noticed."
